answer: The frozen corpus indicates that oral magnesium supplementation was tested in older adults, with one double-blind randomized trial showing no statistically significant difference in total sleep time between magnesium and placebo groups (P = 0.37) [2][1]. A systematic review of oral magnesium for insomnia in older adults identified three randomized trials involving 151 participants but concluded the evidence quality was low to very low [3]. The corpus also documents a separate study of magnesium L-threonate in adults with self-reported sleep problems, explicitly noting this form cannot be generalized to other magnesium salts [4]. Additionally, a clinical trial of magnesium gluconate in adults with diabetes and insomnia is registered but results are not publicly available in the frozen registry snapshot [5]. Limitations include the absence of reported elemental magnesium dosing details in the primary trial, preventing precise dose comparison, and the low-to-very-low evidence quality across studies, which precludes definitive conclusions about efficacy or safety [1][3]. No other limitations are explicitly stated in the supplied passages.
